orders.description: Plaintiff’s appeal from the January 5, 2015 order.
orders.trial_court_action: Granted defendant’s summary-judgment motion and dismissed the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly slipped on snow or ice in defendant’s parking lot. She contended the snowfall was light and challenged defendant’s snow-removal practices through a property-management expert.

legal_issues.finding: Snow/ice removal duty was suspended until a reasonable time after the storm, defeating the expert’s practices-based challenge.

Plaintiff failed to raise an issue that a preexisting condition caused the fall and defendant had actual or constructive notice of it. The court did not separately establish either notice category as a fact.

Plaintiff failed to raise an issue that a preexisting condition caused the fall and defendant had actual or constructive notice of it. The court did not separately establish either notice category as a fact.
Defendant established a storm in progress. Light snowfall did not defeat the defense; plaintiff raised no triable preexisting-condition-with-notice issue.
Property-management expert’s assertions of departures from customary removal practices did not raise an issue because the duty was suspended during the storm.

evidence_discussed.description: Plaintiff’s property-management expert criticized snow/ice removal practices; opinion format unstated.

quality.notes: Defendant’s parking lot and its snow-removal practices support private control; no title, store use, customer role or date inferred. No meteorologist or weather records identified. Light snowfall remains storm evidence, not proof the storm ceased.

evidence.quote: It is hereby ordered that the order so appealed from is unanimously affirmed without costs.
Plaintiff commenced this action seeking damages for injuries she sustained when she slipped and fell on snow or ice in defendant’s parking lot.
Appeal from an order of the Supreme Court, Monroe County (Thomas A. Stander, J.), entered January 5, 2015. The order granted the motion of defendant for summary judgment and dismissed the complaint.

“Defendant met its initial burden by establishing that a storm was in progress at the time of the accident and, thus, that it ‘had no duty to remove the snow [or] ice until a reasonable time ha[d] elapsed after cessation of the storm’ ” (Witherspoon v Tops Mkts., LLC, 128 AD3d 1541, 1541 [2015]).

In opposition to the motion, plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue of fact “whether the accident was caused by a slippery condition at the location where the plaintiff fell that existed prior to the storm, as opposed to precipitation from the storm in progress, and that the defendant had actual or constructive notice of the preexisting condition” (Meyers v Big Six Towers, Inc., 85 AD3d 877, 878 [2011]).
Contrary to plaintiffs contention, evidence that it was only snowing lightly at the time of the accident does not render the storm in progress doctrine inapplicable.

The assertions of plaintiff’s property management expert that defendant’s snow and ice removal practices deviated from accepted and customary practices of property management also failed to raise an issue of fact, inasmuch as “defendant’s duty in this regard was suspended until a reasonable period of time after the storm ended” (Wood v Converse, 263 AD2d 860, 861 [1999]).
Supreme Court properly granted defendant’s motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

orders.description: Defendant’s appeal from the April 30, 2020 order.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly tripped and fell inside premises owned by the defendant Roman Catholic church. The specific interior location and alleged hazard are not described.

legal_issues.finding: Defendant failed to establish that plaintiff did not know the cause; the burden never shifted. The opinion does not identify the cause or evidence format.

quality.notes: Express church ownership supports private religious premises. Do not invent a defect, deposition, injured role or accident date from the successful opposition to dismissal. Unchanged rules for 2022 opinion.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is affirmed, with costs.
The plaintiff allegedly was injured when she tripped and fell inside premises owned by the defendant.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, the defendant appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Queens County (Richard G. Latin, J.), dated April 30, 2020. The order denied the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.
Sara Rozo, Respondent, v Roman Catholic Church of the Precious Blood, Appellant.
Here, viewing the evidence in the light most favorable to the plaintiff as the nonmoving party, the defendant failed to establish, prima facie, that the plaintiff did not know what caused her to fall
Accordingly, the Supreme Court properly denied the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

orders.description: Plaintiffs’ limited appeal from the December 3, 2008 order.
orders.trial_court_action: Granted defendants’ dismissal cross motions while substituting decedent’s representative.

facts.factual_summary: Decedent allegedly tripped and fell in July 2003 at premises leased by Manducatis Restaurant and owned by the Cerbone trust. The fall mechanism and exact location are unstated.

legal_issues.finding: Summary-judgment cross motions made during the death/substitution stay should not have been considered. The new representative had no opportunity to oppose them; remittal permits proper service, opposition and merits determination.

quality.notes: Private leased/owned premises and trip are clear, but appellate decision solely addresses stay/substitution procedure. Preserve reversed/null; consequential remittal is not mixed or remand-only. One appealed order covers separate cross motions. July 2003 remains partial date; no precise premises use, hazard or injured role inferred.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is reversed insofar as appealed from, on the law, with one bill of costs to the plaintiffs payable by the defendants appearing separately and filing separate briefs, and the matter is remitted to the Supreme Court, Queens County, for further proceedings consistent herewith.

In July 2003 the plaintiffs’ decedent, Guido Aceto (hereinafter the decedent), allegedly was injured when he tripped and fell at the premises leased by the defendant Manducatis Restaurant, Inc. (hereinafter Manducatis), and owned by the defendant Vincenzo Cerbone Revocable Living Trust. Manducatis is owned by the defendants Vincenzo Cerbone and Ida Cerbone.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, etc., the plaintiffs appeal, as limited by their brief, from so much of an order of the Supreme Court, Queens County (Rosengarten, J.), entered December 3, 2008, as granted those branches of the cross motion of the defendants Vincenzo Cerbone, Vincenzo Cerbone Revocable Living Trust, and Ida Cerbone, and the separate cross motion of the defendant Manducatis Restaurant, Inc., which were for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against each of them.

Here, while the Supreme Court, in the order appealed from, first substituted a personal representative of the decedent’s estate in place of the decedent as a plaintiff and also granted the cross motions seeking summary judgment dismissing the complaint, it was error for the Supreme Court to have considered the cross motions since the cross motions were made at a time when the stay was still in effect

Moreover, the personal representative of the decedent’s estate, the newly-substituted plaintiff, was not afforded an opportunity to oppose the defendants’ cross motions since she was not a party at the time that the cross motions were made.

Accordingly, we remit the matter to Supreme Court, Queens County, for further proceedings, including service by the defendants, if they be so advised, of the cross motions upon the plaintiffs, for the submission of answering papers, if any, pursuant to CPLR 2214, and for a détermination of the cross motions on the merits.

orders.description: Plaintiff’s limited appeal from the October 13, 2020 order concerning Food Parade.
orders.trial_court_action: Granted dismissal of the complaint against Food Parade.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly slipped in a recently mopped supermarket bathroom. The opinion does not describe the mopping substance or any particular warning’s form or placement.

legal_issues.finding: Defendants’ own submissions raised issues whether Food Parade gave any warning about the potentially hazardous bathroom and whether a warning adequately identified the interior hazard; initial burden unmet.

quality.notes: Supermarket interior and Food Parade’s warning responsibility support private control without specifying title/lease. Recently mopped does not identify water or a particular negligent cleaning method. No evidence format or customer role inferred; March 8, 2019 is commencement, not accident date. Unchanged rules for 2023 opinion.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is reversed insofar as appealed from, on the law, with costs, and that branch of the defendants' motion which was for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against the defendant Food Parade, Inc., is denied.
The plaintiff allegedly sustained injuries when he slipped and fell in the bathroom of a supermarket in Nassau County that had been recently mopped.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, the plaintiff appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Nassau County (Denise L. Sher, J.), entered October 13, 2020. The order, insofar as appealed from, granted that branch of the defendants' motion which was for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against the defendant Food Parade, Inc.

Here, the defendants failed to establish their prima facie entitlement to judgment as a matter of law dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against Food Parade. The evidence submitted by the defendants in support of the motion raised triable issues of fact as to whether Food Parade provided any warning about a potentially hazardous condition in the bathroom and whether any warning that was provided adequately gave notice that there was a hazardous condition inside the bathroom
Accordingly, the Supreme Court should have denied that branch of the defendants' motion which was for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against Food Parade.

orders.description: Defendants’ appeal from the October 17, 2014 order.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly slipped on black ice on a driveway located on defendants’ premises. Their branch manager described a customary morning inspection practice, without evidence it was followed on the accident day.

legal_issues.finding: Defendants supplied no personal-knowledge affidavit/testimony establishing last driveway inspection or preaccident condition. A customary morning practice without proof of implementation that day did not negate notice.

evidence_discussed.description: Branch manager’s testimony described usual inspection practice, not an inspection on the accident day; testimony format unspecified.

quality.notes: Driveway expressly on defendants’ premises plus employee/branch-manager inspection responsibility supports private control, unlike a merely abutting public route. Exact use and title are unstated; driveway is other location. No inspection records or weather evidence identified. Third-party caption does not change direct negligence merits.

evidence.quote: Order, Supreme Court, New York County (Joan A. Madden, J.), entered October 17, 2014, which denied defendants' motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint, unanimously affirmed, without costs.
in this action where plaintiff alleges that he slipped and fell on a patch of black ice on a driveway located on defendants' premises.

Defendants did not demonstrate that they lacked constructive notice of the icy condition since they did not proffer an affidavit or testimony based on personal knowledge as to when its employees last inspected the driveway or as to the driveway's condition prior to the accident

The testimony of defendants' branch manager as to his usual and customary practice of inspecting the premises each morning does not satisfy defendants' burden of showing that they lacked notice of the alleged condition of the driveway prior to the accident, as there was no evidence to show that the manager's customary practice was followed on the day of the accident
